items.title: Thanks Google! I am cancelling my Claude subscription...

In this video, I'll review Gemini 4 Neon, Google's new mid-tier coding model released on November 18 between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon, starting with its quiet rollout, $3 and $15 pricing, 1M context window, four thinking levels, and hands-on behavior in Antigravity CLI. Then I'll run it through all six KingBench 4 one-prompt app builds — a Rust Game Boy, DS, and 3DS emulator, a Go Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a QMK VIA keyboard configurator, Pokémon Red, and a Rust Fitbit desktop app — showing what actually worked, what broke, and how it landed at #2 out of 18 models for just $20.36. Next, I'll break down its coding habits and blind spots across 108.7 minutes and show how I pair Neon with Hydrogen, Panda Router, and a 9 out of 10 Council gate inside PandaCode, our free open-source multi-agent desktop app. Finally, I'll compare Gemini 4 Neon head-to-head against GPT-6.2 So
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. Google just quietly pushed out Gemini 4 Neon today, November 18th, pitched right in the middle between Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon. Yet, on my six project King Bench 4 test, this middle model beat Carbon and Argon, passed Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.2 Astra and landed at number two overall behind only Claude Fable 5.2 at less than 1/10 of Fable's API cost. At the same time, its keyboard app resets your keyboard into bootloader mode and its Fitbit app talks to an API Google shut down two weeks ago. So, how good is Gemini 4 Neon really? How does it compare with Soul, Astra, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 and is it actually worth using? What makes this release even stranger is how it rolled out. The API Docs, AI Studio, Vertex Enterprise Docs, and Antigravity CLI all went live before Google's own blog post or DeepMind model card, which still returned a 404 page on launch afternoon. First, let's look at pricing specs and what Neon feels like. It costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens including thinking plus 15 cents per million for automatic cash reads, a 95% discount. There is no explicit caching or free tier, so you need paid API billing or Google AI Pro or Ultra. Here's the catch. Neon has no intro discount while Carbon and Argon stay at $2 and $10 until November 30th before jumping to $4 and $20 on December 1st. So, for November, Neon costs 50% more per token than Carbon. On paper, Neon packs a unified 1 million token window, 64,000 output tokens per hop, long decode up to 1 million via background hops, and four thinking levels from low to extra high. Unlike Carbon and Argon which stop at high in 10 high versus low probes in Antigravity CLI, Neon had zero preamble yapping and started straight at the Unlike Hydrogen at 8% reasoning tokens, Neon spent 56 to 81% on thinking, catching prototype collisions, SQLite deferred lock traps, and go single flight panics while refusing fake Python 3.13 APIs and September 2026 auction traps. Low saves money on routine edits while high earns its keep on hard bug. Now let's get into King Bench 4 so we can see how Neon builds real software. King Bench 4 gives a model six big projects with one prompt each and zero follow-ups or fixes. Those six apps are a Game Boy DS and 3DS emulator in Rust, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a yellow QMK via keyboard configurator, the first chapter of Pokémon Red, and a Fitbit desktop app with a Rust backend. Missing or fake features get zero and any container escape caps the runtime at three out of 10. I ran all six concurrently in Anti-Gravity CLI version 1.5.11 at high effort with no time, turn, or token limits. Keep the harness caveat in mind too because Hydrogen and Carbon ran in open code, Argon ran in Devon, Fable, and Opus ran in Claude code with a 60-minute cutoff on Opus, and Soul and Astra ran in Codex CLI. Let's start with the first app, the Rust emulator, where Neon scored 4.3 out of 10. That is the third highest emulator score on the entire benchmark behind Fable 5.2 at 5.8 and Argon at 5.2 and ahead of Carbon at 4.2, Opus 5.5 at 3.7, Hydrogen at 3.2, GPT 6.2, Soul at 1.6, and GPT 6.2 Astra at 0.0 because Astra downloaded third-party binaries. Neon built Trireme with real execution cores across all three consoles, hitting over 4,000 frames per second on Game Boy, deterministic save states and rewind, and working built-in demos for Game Boy, DS, and 3DS. Where it breaks is on external ROMs. External DS test ROMs crash with a stack overflow because 32-bit hardware register reads loop infinitely and DS interrupts never reach handlers. The 3DS Pica 200 GPU skips vertex shaders, textures, and depth while running at roughly 7% of the real frame cycle budget and GameBoy fails two interrupt timing edge cases. So it delivers three real engines with working demos even though external DS and 3DS software breaks. Next up is the Docker alternative which Neon built as Kestrel in pure Go with zero external dependencies. Before Caps, Kestrel earned 4.75 out of 10 with working multi-stage cached builds, local registry V2 push and pull, APFS copy-on-write clones, diff and commit, and a clean pass under go test -race. Here is the irony though. Google's launch docs claim Neon writes code with fewer security vulnerabilities. Yet a hostile image with symlinks escapes straight onto your host disk in seven places during load and create. That triggers the exact same 3.0 cap as Fable 5.2, carbon, argon, and hydrogen, while GPT 6.2 Astra at 5.0, GPT 6.2 Sol at 4.7, and Opus 5.5 at 4.6 avoided that escape. On top of that, detached run -d -p tears down port listeners when the CLI exits and colon RO mounts stay writable on macOS, clean go plumbing, but an unverified Linux runtime with seven host disk escape. The third app is the 3D room designer where Neon scored a strong 8.5 out of 10. That ties Claude Opus 5.5 at 8.5, sits behind only Fable 5.2 at 9.2 and DeepSeek V4.1 flash at 8.8 and beats argon at 8.1, GPT 6.2 Astra at 7.6, hydrogen at 6.6, GPT 6.2 Sol at 6.4, and carbon at 6.3. Neon built Atelier 3D with real-time room dimensions, rebuilding geometry, 15 furniture types, 13 procedural PBR finishes, colored shadows, custom GLSL shaders with GTO and bloom, smooth 60 frames per second on 30 items, and zero WebGL memory leaks. Finally, fixing Argon's leak, the defects are still easy to spot. Rotated or oversized furniture collapses its clamping bounds to zero and pokes half a meter through walls. Unvalidated JSON crashes. Texture lookup on an unknown floor material. The sun beam plane leaves a seam through walls. And a 390 pixel mobile screen squeezes the canvas to 70 pixels wide. Still, on desktop, it is one of the sharpest 3D editors on the bench. Fourth is the Vault QMK keyboard configurator, where Neon scored 6.2 out of 10. That beats GPT 6.2 Sol at 5.9, Carbon at 4.9, Hydrogen at 3.5, and Argon at 2.4 while trailing Fable 5.2 at 7.6, Opus 5.5 at 7.5, and GPT 6.2 Astra at 7.0. Its solar yellow and amber Obsidian UI looks cohesive, and it sends real 32 byte Web Hit VI version 12 packets for key maps, encoders, layout options, and macros against our virtual keyboard. Then the firmware bugs show up, and one is painful. Clicking factory EEPROM reset sends hex 0B instead of 0A, which tells QMK to jump straight into bootloader mode instead of wiping settings. Custom lighting channels shift by plus one. Switch matrix polling reads the wrong byte offset, modifier keys, or in hex 010 sent, so shift and command turn into control combinations, and short JSON imports wipe your keys. Nice UI and real VI packets right up until wrong byte codes bite you. The fifth app is Pokémon Red, and Neon scored 8.4 out of 10, tying Claude Fable 5.2. That beats Carbon at 8.2, GPT 6.2 Astra at 7.7, GPT 6.2 Sol at 5.6, Opus 5.5 at 3.0, and Hydrogen at 3.0. Unlike Fable, which refused Pokémon IP and built Kith bound, Neon actually built Pokémon Red across all 18 interconnected maps from Red's bedroom through Route 1, Viridian City, Oak's parcel, and Viridian Forest to beating Brock for the Boulder badge at 60 frames per second, including blackout recovery and working start menu saves. There are still clear bugs. Dialogue cuts off after three lines with no pagination, missing bitmap font brackets and arrows leave blank spaces in menus, and learning a new move gets skipped on a final foe knockout. Also, Neon's own walkthrough test suppressed wild encounters and injected a level 15 Squirtle, even though our independent play test proved the real game beats Brock fairly without cheating. The last app is the Fitbit desktop app, Pulse Sync, where Neon scored 7.5 out of 10. That is the second best Fitbit app on the whole benchmark behind only Fable 5.2 at 8.0 and ahead of Opus 5.5 at 7.4, GPT 6.2, Astra at 6.3, Hydrogen at 5.6, GPT 6.2, Soul at 5.4, and Carbon at 5.4. It is a real Tory version two Rust and SQLite desktop app with zero JavaScript mock fallback, accurate trim, strain recovery and sleep coach math, and working takeout, TCX, GPX, and CSV imports. Here is the key contrast with Fable 5.2. Fable checked live docs and used the Google Health API. Neon coded from memory against the dead Fitbit Web API. Google shut down on November 2nd, swallows failed HTTP replies as success true, invents defaults like 7,000 steps and 69 recovery on partial days, duplicates workouts on reimport, and stores OAuth tokens in plain text SQLite. Great offline analytics undone by coding against a dead API from memory. Now let's look at the final scoreboard in the bill. Gemini 4 Neon finishes with 37.9 out of 60 or 63.2%, placing number two out of all 18 models tested behind only Fable 5.2 at 42. It beats Opus 5.5 at 34.7, GPT 6, Astra at 33.9, GPT 6.2 Astra at 33.6, GPT 6.1 Soul at 33.0, Argon at 32.6, Carbon at 32.0, GPT 6.2 Soul at 29.6, and Hydrogen at 24.9 and the bill is wild. Neon used 27.1 million tokens total, including 25 million cash reads at 15 cents per million and 859,000 output tokens including thinking for just $20.36 at list prices. Fable 5.2 burned 212 million tokens for $222, nearly 11 times more. GPT-6.2 Astra costs $28, Soul costs $10, and Carbon costs $23.04 on intro pricing from 76.5 million tokens. These Neon tokens would cost $27.15 at Carbon's December rates and over $32 on Opus 5.4. Beyond the scores, Neon has a clear personality across 108.7 minutes and 244 steps averaging 18 minutes per app. First, it is virtually silent while working, dropping only three short progress lines across six runs. Second, it writes 70 to 95% of a project cleanly in one pass, creating 201 unique files with only three full file rewrites, way cleaner than Fable's 311 rewrites, followed by 62 surgical edits and tight compiler loops on emulator and room designer. It even opened its own rendered screenshots to inspect frames and lighting. Third, it used zero sub agents, so it never walks away from unfinished background workers like Fable did on its 3DS agent. Its clear blind spot is coding from training memory without checking live external changes like the November 22 Fit Bit shutdown or QMK byte codes. It also tests like a happy path builder rather than a hostile attacker, missing seven SimLink escapes and still over claims in final summaries, bragging about sanitized JSON imports and a full Pokémon walkthrough when its test injected a level 15 Squirtle. And that brings us straight to Panda Code, our free open source multi agent desktop app running Anti-Gravity CLI, Claude Code, Codex, Open Code, and Kimi in one workspace. Anti-Gravity CLI version 1.5.11 already ships Gemini 4 Neon and Orchestrator Neon out of the box. Inside PandaCode team mode, pairing Neon at $3 and $15 with hydrogen at 1.50 and 7.50 is a killer combo because Neon brings the reasoning horsepower hydrogen lacked while hydrogen knocks out parallel worker tasks for pennies. Panda router also keeps costs low by sending routine work to cheap models like hydrogen, Sol, or Terra and escalating to Neon, Opus 5.5 or Fable 5.2 only when checks fail. Better yet, PandaCode's council with a 9 out of 10 gate directly fixes Neon's blind spots. Read only reviewers on Opus 5.5 Fable or Astra inspect Neon's build and catch the dead Fitbit API, the hex 0B bootloader jump, the injected squirtle test, and the symlink escapes before anything ships. So where does Neon stand against its rivals? Against GPT 6.2 Sol at 29.6 and GPT 6.1 Sol at 33.0 Sol is half the price at $2 and $10 and beat Neon on container safety at 4.7 and 5.0 against $3. Yet Neon beats 6.2 Sol on five of six apps by 8.3 points. Against GPT 6.2 Astra at 33.6 it is a blowout because Astra charges $8.40 scored zero on emulator by downloading binaries, skipped browser checks, and finished 4.3 points behind while costing $27.93 against $20.36. Against Claude Opus 5.5 at 34.7 and $4 and $20 it is closer. Opus is safer on container and protocol edges and shines on Claude Code Max. Yet on the API Neon is 25% cheaper, has zero cash right fees, finishes faster, and beat Opus overall. Against Claude Fable 5.2 at $42 and $8 and $40 Fable stays the quality king on the $200 ultra plan while on the API Neon gets 90% of Fable score for under 1/10 of the bill beating Argon at 32.6 and Carbon at 32.0 as Google's best coding model today. So, is Gemini 4 Neon actually worth it? Yes. For API builders, AI Studio Pro and Ultra users and multi-agent workflows, is Google's most worthwhile Gemini 4 release yet with two caveats. Until November 30, Carbon is still $2 and $10 on intro pricing. Though Neon actually costs less on our full run because it uses nearly three times fewer tokens. And on December 1 when Carbon jumps to $4 and $20, Neon becomes an easy pick. Second, never trust it blindly on security boundaries, recently changed APIs or hardware bytecodes without a reviewer or council pass on top and drop it to lower medium for quick edits so you do not waste $15 thinking tokens. Use Fable on Ultra for your hardest builds, Opus 5.5 for Claude code daily driving, Solar Hydrogen for cheap parallel workers, and Gemini 4 Neon as the new number one price to performance coding API model. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. [music] If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by [music] clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
